extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, moral/political theory, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Characterizing the proper method for creating and applying practical rules (arts, policy, and ethics) grounded in scientific knowledge and teleological justification. Covers when to form rules, how to justify ends, and how to balance completeness and usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art vs Science (imperative vs indicative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperative mood is the characteristic of art, as distinguished from science. Whatever speaks in rules, or precepts, not in assertions respecting matters of fact, is art; and ethics, or morality, is properly a portion of the art corresponding to the sciences of human nature and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prescriptive statements (rules, duties) as part of 'art' (practice) and descriptive statements as belonging to 'science' (inquiries into the course of nature). Do not conflate the two: rules prescribe ends and actions; science investigates causes and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different methods for rule-application (judge) vs rule-formation (legislator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge is to interpret and apply an existing rule by ratiocination or syllogism; the legislator, who frames rules, must take into consideration the reasons or grounds of the maxim rather than merely arguing down from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the task is application, use interpretive syllogistic reasoning. When the task is to create or revise rules, examine the scientific/theoretical grounds and reasons underlying the rule rather than treating the rule as final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of art must be founded on theorems of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasons of a maxim of policy, or of any other rule of art, can be no other than the theorems of the corresponding science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art supplies the desirable end; science investigates the causes and conditions and returns theorems about combinations of circumstances that will produce the end. Practitioners should transform scientific theorems into precepts only when the scientific basis is adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert incomplete scientific truths into precepts prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem or speculative truth is not ripe for being turned into a precept, until the whole, and not a part merely, of the operation which belongs to science, has been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure negative conditions and counteracting causes are explored before forming a rule. If a rule fails because overlooked counteracting causes exist, re-open the scientific investigation to identify all relevant conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules should be provisional and aimed at ordinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sake of convenience, rules must be formed from something less than an ideally perfect theory; the rules of art do not attempt to comprise more conditions than require to be attended to in ordinary cases; and are therefore always imperfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules to be usable and memorable for common situations, but treat them as provisional aids. In complex social or political affairs, continually refer back to the underlying scientific principles to determine exceptions or needed modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing policy solely from universal practical maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to deduce conduct for particular cases from supposed universal practical maxims without constantly referring back to the principles of the speculative science; setting up unbending practical principles as general rules is mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reason down from abstract universal principles (the 'geometrical' method) to particular policy without empirical/theoretical examination; check whether adherence to a principle produces undesirable consequences or conflicts with other ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: An art must include the scientific propositions that justify its rules (intermediate principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: An art, or a body of art, consists of the rules, together with as much of the speculative propositions as comprises the justification of those rules. There is need of a set of intermediate scientific truths ... destined to serve as the generalia or first principles of the various arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting or teaching an art, include the intermediate principles (general relations between means and ends) drawn from science so practitioners can understand when and why rules apply and how to adapt them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and justification of ends belongs to Art (teleology required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of the end itself belongs exclusively to Art ... The only one of the premises which Art supplies, is the original major premise, which asserts that the attainment of the given end is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define and justify the ends that rules aim to achieve; science alone cannot determine what ought to be pursued. Practitioners must supply the initial normative premise before applying scientific theorems to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate teleological standard: conduciveness to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principle to which all rules of practice ought to conform, and the test by which they should be tried, is that of conduciveness to the happiness of mankind, or rather, of all sentient beings; in other words, that the promotion of happiness is the ultimate principle of Teleology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the promotion of (sentient) happiness as the controlling standard for evaluating ends and rules. This is offered as the preferred single standard, though it need not be the sole proximate end in every action; temper application with consideration of long-term and aggregate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for virtuous actions that sacrifice immediate happiness if justified by net effect
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many virtuous actions ... by which happiness in the particular instance is sacrificed ... But conduct of which this can be truly asserted, admits of justification only because it can be shown that, on the whole, more happiness will exist in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rules that prescribe self-denying or painful actions, require justification demonstrating that such conduct cultivates dispositions or conditions that increase overall happiness in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific theory cannot substitute for decisions about ends
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific observer or reasoner, merely as such, is not an adviser for practice. His part is only to show that certain consequences follow from certain causes ... Whether the ends themselves are such as ought to be pursued ... it is no part of his business as a cultivator of science to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let technically excellent scientific analysis be taken as sufficient for normative recommendations; complement scientific findings with explicit teleological argument when proposing policies or ethical prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: There must be a single ultimate standard of conduct for consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some standard by which to determine the goodness or badness, absolute and comparative, of ends ... And whatever that standard is, there can be but one; for if there were several ultimate principles of conduct, the same conduct might be approved by one ... and condemned by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a single overarching criterion (the author advocates happiness) to serve as the umpire among conflicting rules and to avoid irreconcilable moral judgments; otherwise introduce a higher-level principle to resolve conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance completeness and usability when formulating rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If all the counteracting contingencies, whether of frequent or of rare occurrence, were included, the rules would be too cumbrous to be apprehended and remembered by ordinary capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing prescriptive rules, weigh the trade-off between exhaustively listing conditions and creating manageable rules. Provide guidance on frequent exceptions and encourage practitioners to consult scientific bases for atypical cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey available resources and condense into general propositions linking means to ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After framing the most comprehensive possible conception of the end ... there remains to be taken, a general survey of the resources which can be commanded for realizing this set of conditions; and when the result of this survey has been embodied in the fewest and most extensive propositions possible, those propositions will ... constitute the general scientific theory of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practical design, map conditions required for the effect, inventory available means, and express the relation between means and ends in broad, general propositions that practitioners can apply and from which specific methods follow as corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a rule fails, reopen scientific investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any counteracting cause, overlooked by the theorem, takes place, the rule will be at fault ... there is nothing for it but to turn back and finish the scientific process which should have preceded the formation of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat rule failure as diagnostic: rather than arguing about the rule, investigate the missing or mis-specified scientific conditions. Update the scientific theory and then reformulate the rule to incorporate the newly discovered conditions.
